issues.item: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: The profile is not coherent with a toxic chemical exposure trauma. The selected Threat items are dominated by interpersonal/being-followed danger themes ('someone is following me', lock checking) rather than contamination, health deterioration, environmental exposure, or bodily harm themes that would fit chemical exposure.

issues.item: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: The Maladaptive Strategy item 'Never Alone' is also strongly interpersonal/assault-focused and is hard to reconcile with toxic chemical exposure. 'Avoid Conflict' similarly targets confrontation rather than exposure-related danger, and is not plausibly linked to the selected Threat items or trauma type.

issues.item: Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
issues.explanation: For toxic chemical exposure, 'Never Alone with another person' is hard to reconcile clinically: it implies fear of interpersonal danger rather than contamination, bodily harm, or environmental exposure. No Trigger, Memory, or Appraisal items support an interpersonal-assault formulation.

issues.item: Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Conflict' also points to interpersonal threat management rather than consequences of chemical exposure. With no corroborating interpersonal threat, appraisal, or memory content, this strategy appears misaligned with the trauma type and the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
issues.explanation: For toxic chemical exposure, avoiding conflict is not a plausible trauma-linked maladaptive strategy unless supported by appraisals about blame, authority, or interpersonal danger, which are absent here. It appears clinically disconnected from the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building
issues.explanation: Avoiding being alone is hard to reconcile with the stated threat pattern. The threat items emphasize generalized unsafety and checking the physical environment, but not collapse, contamination, or medical emergency fears that would make solitude specifically dangerous after chemical exposure.

vignette: Rahul, a 52-year-old HVAC technician of South Eastern Asian descent, had been working on a construction site when disaster struck. A leak in one of the chemical storage tanks released a toxic cloud that enveloped him and several coworkers. Rahul remembered the searing pain in his eyes and lungs, the sound of panicked screams, and the feeling of being unable to escape. As he stumbled out into fresh air, he saw one of his colleagues collapse, never to get up again. The incident left an indelible mark on Rahul's psyche. Even when others assured him that the site was safe now, even when his wife, Nalini, tried to comfort him at home, he couldn't shake off the feeling of perpetual danger. His body remained tense and ready to react, always poised for flight or fight. "I just can't trust it," Rahul would tell himself, his mind racing with worst-case scenarios whenever someone said he was safe. This persistent sense of threat began to dictate his daily life. Rahul started avoiding anything that could be stressful - he stopped taking on new projects at work and turned down social invitations from friends and family. "What if I get overwhelmed?" he would think, envisioning himself losing control in a crowded room or under pressure on the job site. He also became increasingly uncomfortable with being alone, whether it was in his workshop or even in their home when Nalini went out for errands. His mind would start racing with catastrophic thoughts - "What if someone breaks in?" or "What if there's another accident?" To mitigate these fears, Rahul developed an exhausting routine of checking doors and windows multiple times a day. As time passed, the habits he formed to cope with his perceived danger became ingrained. Rahul avoided relaxing altogether because it felt like letting his guard down. He couldn't bear the thought of being off-guard, even for a moment. His wife noticed that he never seemed to unwind anymore - no more lazy Sundays watching cricket or playing guitar as he used to. "I'm just too tired," Rahul would say, though Nalini knew it was more than exhaustion. One day, after months of struggling with his ever-present anxiety and increasingly erratic behavior, Rahul's wife sat him down for a heart-to-heart talk. She expressed her concerns about the toll this was taking on their relationship and his overall well-being. For the first time, Rahul realized he wasn't just living in fear - he was also losing himself to it. The thought sent a jolt of recognition through him: he needed help. That's when Rahul finally reached out for professional support, hoping to break free from this suffocating cycle of threat and avoidance that had taken over his life. As he sat in the therapist's office, recounting his story and the fears that now defined him, Rahul couldn't shake off the feeling that he was still trapped - waiting for the next disaster to strike, unsure if he'd ever be able to trust safety again.
